cards.back: $$ \bar{x}_{\text{treatment}} - \bar{x}_{\text{control}} $$ A positive difference means the treatment group had a higher average.
cards.front: How do you calculate the [[kw:experimental difference of means]]?

cards.back: The treatment group mean is [[imp:lower]] than the control group mean. Example: music therapy reducing depression scores.
cards.front: What does a negative experimental difference indicate?
Why might an observed difference between two small groups not be meaningful?
cards.back: It could be due to [[imp:random chance]] rather than a real treatment effect. Resampling helps assess how likely a difference of that size is under chance alone.
A method where the original data from both groups are combined, then repeatedly split at random into new 'control' and 'treatment' groups to see what differences occur by chance.

cards.front: In resampling, do you draw the new groups with or without replacement?
cards.back: [[imp:Without replacement]]. Each original data point is used exactly once per resample, preserving the overall distribution.

cards.front: What is the hypothesis being tested when we resample?
cards.back: The [[kw:null hypothesis]]: that the treatment has no effect, i.e., the true difference between the groups is 0.

cards.front: What does the resampling distribution show?
cards.back: A histogram of the differences of means from many random reassignments of the combined data. It shows what differences occur just by [[imp:chance]] when there is no treatment effect.

cards.front: Where is the resampling distribution centered?
cards.back: Near [[imp:0]], because the random splitting simulates no true difference between the groups.

cards.front: How do you decide if the experimental difference is significant?
cards.back: If the observed difference falls in the [[imp:tail]] of the resampling distribution (outside the middle 90% or 95%), it is unlikely due to chance, so we reject the 'no effect' hypothesis.
We [[imp:fail to reject]] the hypothesis of no effect. There is not enough evidence to say the treatment works.
cards.front: If the experimental difference is near the center of the resampling distribution, what do we conclude?
In the tomato supplement example, the observed difference was 0.32 kg. Only 4% of resampled differences were larger. What was the conclusion?
cards.back: The difference was statistically significant; we concluded the soil supplement [[imp:does increase]] tomato yield.
The observed difference is consistent with chance variation. It does [[imp:not]] prove the treatment has zero effect, only that we lack strong evidence of an effect.
cards.front: What does it mean to 'fail to reject' the null hypothesis?
Why do we need a large number of resamples (e.g., 200)?
cards.back: To build a [[imp:stable histogram]] that accurately reflects the distribution of chance differences. A few resamples are not enough to see the pattern.

cards.front: What is the purpose of a double dot plot in a two‑sample experiment?
cards.back: To visually compare the [[imp:distributions]] of the two groups. It helps see overlap, central tendency, and spread, and whether the means seem different.

cards.front: If the middle 90% of resampled differences ranges from −2.1 to 2.1, and the experimental difference is −2.3, what is the conclusion?
cards.back: −2.3 is outside the central 90%, so it is an extreme result. We reject the 'no effect' hypothesis and conclude the treatment has a significant effect.
